purpose: Treat setting as a meaning-bearing part of the witnessed moment, not a background field.
principles: Setting changes what is seen, who sees it, what words are available, which bodies are touched, and who controls the next step.
A hospice bedroom, ICU bay, ED family room, prison cell, shelter, street, disaster site, birth room, funeral home, and morgue cannot be collapsed into one universal deathbed.
The archive should index setting before orienting a reader; many panic-search readers are really asking what kind of room they have entered.
No setting is automatically a good death or a bad death. Place is evidence, not moral verdict.

clusters.name: home and familiar rooms
what_the_setting_changes: family may be first witness
equipment becomes domestic furniture
pets, mail, neighbors, money, estrangement, and household labor enter the scene
body may remain in the home during initial calls and waiting
clusters.danger: romanticizing home as inherently better, safer, cheaper, or more authentic

clusters.name: hospice facility and hospice house
what_the_setting_changes: staff are practiced around death
family may feel relief and guilt together
room is designed for dying but still must be personalized
symptom crises may be easier to contain
clusters.danger: making hospice facility transfer feel like failure

clusters.name: hospital ward, ED, ICU, and isolation settings
what_the_setting_changes: machines and monitors shape perception
emergency and institutional language enter
family presence may be mediated or restricted
strangers may deliver the news
clusters.danger: treating institutional death as less human or automatically failed

clusters.name: ambulance, doorway, and prehospital threshold
what_the_setting_changes: home becomes an emergency scene
documents and wishes may need rapid interpretation by others
sirens, uniforms, and transport pressure change family perception
clusters.danger: turning EMS records into emergency instructions

clusters.name: care home, nursing home, assisted living, and residential facilities
what_the_setting_changes: staff may know the body better than distant relatives
routines and shift changes shape witnessing
home-like belongings coexist with facility policy
clusters.danger: making facility death invisible or assuming neglect without evidence

clusters.name: street, shelter, custody, public, violent, overdose, and suicide-adjacent settings
what_the_setting_changes: privacy may be absent
official systems may control body and record
stigma and criminalization can replace personhood
public narrative may arrive before family narrative
clusters.danger: poverty, custody, method, violence, or spectacle replacing the person

clusters.name: disaster, war, conflict, humanitarian emergency, and unrecovered body contexts
what_the_setting_changes: the body may be delayed, partial, unidentified, or absent
families may receive belongings or data before remains
public-health myths and mass scale can erase individual dignity
clusters.danger: mass scale erasing names, rites, and family truth

clusters.name: maternal, perinatal, neonatal, and pediatric settings
what_the_setting_changes: birth, childhood, school, siblings, and death language collide
memory-making may be offered but must be family-led
child and baby material requires the highest privacy gate
clusters.danger: sentimentality, adult projection, or extraction of child/family material

clusters.name: funeral home, morgue, cemetery, crematory, and disposition settings
what_the_setting_changes: body becomes cared for by another profession
paperwork, identification, preparation, disposition, and worker knowledge enter
family may encounter the body again in a changed room
clusters.danger: technical spectacle, legal advice, or worker invisibility

global_nonclaims: not a claim that any setting guarantees dignity or prevents harm
review_rule: Every public rendering must say which setting it is speaking from and which settings it is not speaking from.
